doc.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: How the record industry changed: artists versus bean counters
summary: Record companies were once run by musicians; now lawyers and accountants run them.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: How has recording changed from then ‘til now for you?

Well, a lot. A lot. I think in the first place, not just recording but the whole music industry. In those days the music industry was wisely left to the artists, you know. The heads of the all the record companies were musicians and artists. They had their business departments with their lawyers and their bookkeepers and their bean counters and all, they were there. But the decisions, you know, that affected the work, were made by artists, so that you had great productivity from all the record companies. The guy, the head of RCA Victor, played with the Philadelphia Symphony Orchestra. He played the clarinet and the bassoon. The head of Columbia Records was Goddard Lieberson, worked in the English music halls. He played piano and would do a dance for you. He was an artist. And it was the same with Decca was headed by Milt Gabler. Milt Gabler opened up his own record company at 17 and knew the names of every great jazz musician, and had a great love for the music. But nowadays, they have taken the lawyers and the accountants and the bean counters from the business department, and put them in charge of the music. Well, put a fox in charge of the chicken coop and see how many chickens you have left at the end of the summer. You’ll have a lot of feathers, but there won’t be no chickens. And that’s the way it is. You’ve got a lot of people recording, but where is the great art?
